A completed run has resolved hundreds of thousands of grants. The obvious next
question is whether that output is itself a database: take the cases cleared
`YES`, treat them as the thing to match against, and see whether new cases
clear.

The answer is yes, with a specific shape and a specific limit. It adds about a
point to the clear rate on the benchmark, it is nearly free to build, and it
cannot discover an organisation it does not already contain. This article covers
what the mechanism is, where in the workflow it runs, what it is worth, and what
its measured precision is -- which, for half the recoveries, is still unknown.

`vignette("matching-dictionaries")` puts this pass beside the alternatives it
competes with -- the active BMF, the augmented BMF, and matchdb's published
tiers -- and is the article to read when choosing *which* database to run
against. This one is about the YES tier alone.

# 1. Two things the question could mean

```{r}
tab(two, col.names = c("reading", "keyed on", "built by", "verdict"))
```

Both were measured, and the difference between them is the whole result. The
first can only ever *remove competitors* -- every row in it is already in the
production reference, so it reaches no EIN the full reference could not. The
second introduces keys the BMF does not hold at all, because filers do not write
registered legal names.

Section 2 reports the first, briefly, because it is a useful diagnostic and
because it is what the question usually means. Sections 3 onward are the
mechanism that ships.

A note on the word *tier*, which this project overloads. A **match tier** is
YES / MAYBE / NO, the cascade's verdict on one grant. A **matchdb tier** is a
published, pre-compiled reference. "The YES tier as a dictionary" means the
first kind.

# 2. The subset reference, and what a subset can do

Take every EIN the benchmark's augmented-BMF arm cleared `YES` -- 2,979
identities over 2,813 distinct EINs -- and carve their BMF rows out of the
production bundle: 9,253 rows, 0.2385% of 3,880,431. Carved rather than rebuilt,
so the keys are byte-identical and the comparison measures competition rather
than normalization.

Re-matching the benchmark's own 4,748 in-scope rows against it:

```{r}
tab(armR, col.names = c("full reference", "no candidate", "YES", "MAYBE", "NO"),
    caption = "Full-reference tier (rows) against mini-reference tier (columns)")
```

**The result worth having is 35 MAYBE to YES**, and in 17 of them (48.6%) the
subset clears to the same EIN the full reference already held as its own top
candidate. On those the production reference had the right answer and the margin
gate would not release it, because competitors kept the margin tight. That is
1.6% of the MAYBE tier, and it is direct support for the reference-side
duplicate finding -- 15.9% of the MAYBE tie band is two BMF rows carrying one
name for one body. The other 18 clear to a different EIN, or the full reference
had no candidate at all; a subset cannot know better than the full reference, so
those are for hand review, not adoption.

Two findings come free with it, and both are worth keeping.

**Shrinking a reference is not monotone.** 16 of the 2,979 full-YES rows (0.5%)
stop clearing against the subset -- 11 drop to MAYBE or NO, 5 find no candidate
-- and 1 clears to a different EIN. Removing rows changes name frequencies and
candidate sets, not just the candidate pool.

**Running it over fresh grants measures coverage, not accuracy.** 50,000 fresh
grant rows against the same 9,253-row subset:

```{r}
tab(armC, col.names = c("", ""))
```

So 3.77% of fresh identities go to one of these 2,813 organisations -- about 29x
enrichment over uniform, since 2,813 is 0.13% of roughly 2.19M distinct
recipient names, but far less concentrated than the headline recipients suggest.
And the precision control says not to quote 3.77% as accuracy: 88.0% survive
contest against the full reference, so about 3.3% is the contest-surviving
figure.

The conclusion: new YES cases do surface, but they are **new grants to
organisations already resolved, not new organisations**. A subset reference
cannot discover an EIN it does not contain. The finding worth keeping is the 17
competition-blocked cases, and the way to pursue those is the reference-side
duplicate work, not a bigger batch.

# 3. The mechanism that ships: a grant-side dictionary

Everything above keyed on the BMF's own strings. The asymmetry that makes the
YES tier worth keeping is that **filers do not write those strings**.
Foundations write recipient names by a convention of their own; the BMF carries
the registered legal name. So a grant the BMF cannot clear may still match a
grant that already cleared.

Over the 312,306 cleared rows of the triangulation run that hold both strings:

```{r}
tab(asym, col.names = c("a cleared row...", "n", "share"))
```

94% of cleared rows are *exactly* some other cleared rendering of the same
organisation, against 47% identical to the BMF name -- and nearly half are
grant-exact while not BMF-exact. That is the gain, and it is a gain of
**frequency, not similarity**: on fuzzy distance the grant side is marginally
*worse* (median 0.960 to the nearest other rendering against 0.967 to the BMF
name, and only 31.7% of distinct renderings are closer to a grant than to the
BMF). A common rendering repeats, so an arriving grant often hits an existing
one exactly. It shows up as exact-key recall, and that distinction governs
everything below.

Where it pays hardest is the acronym and the colloquial name, which the legal
name does not resemble at all -- similarity to the nearest other grant rendering
against similarity to the BMF name:

```{r}
tab(nearest, col.names = c("rendering", "nearest grant", "BMF"))
```

## The key must include the address

Keying on the name alone does not work, and the margin is not close:

```{r}
tab(keyed, col.names = c("key", "distinct keys", "carrying >1 EIN", "worst"))
```

`RONALD MCDONALD HOUSE` carries 31 EINs on a bare name key and `BIG BROTHERS
BIG SISTERS` 29. Adding ZIP5 takes the ambiguity to zero. `pf_grant_dictionary()`
still drops any `(name_key, zip5)` that resolves to more than one EIN rather
than guessing, and reports the count in the `ambiguous_dropped` attribute --
real data never trips it, but a silent collision there would attach one
organisation's EIN to another's grants, which is the one failure this must not
have.

## What it costs to build

```{r}
tab(size, col.names = c("", ""))
```

Nearly free, in other words, and it reads back in under a second. At full scale
the pass is roughly 12 hours single-stream against roughly 186 hours for the
cascade it supplements. Its real cost is not compute; it is the queue in
section 6.

# 4. Where it runs in the workflow

**After the cascade, on what the cascade could not clear, and never instead of
it.** `pf_recover_from_dictionary()` enforces that by only ever retrying rows
whose status is not `YES`.

```
pf_prepare()        read, standardize, resolve the two-line name
  pf_dedup()        collapse grant rows to recipient identities
pf_reference()      the database: matchdb active-observed by default
pf_link()           the staged blocking cascade -> YES / MAYBE / NO
  |
  |--- YES rows ------> pf_grant_dictionary()      build from the cleared tier
  |                             |
  '--- MAYBE + NO ------> pf_recover_from_dictionary()
                                |
                                |--> corroborated: status becomes YES
                                '--> uncorroborated: the `queue` attribute
pf_adjudicate()     the MAYBE sheet, and now the queue beside it
```

In code, after a run:

```{r eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
run  <- pf_run(grants, dir = "data-dev/batches")

# 1. the dictionary, from this run's own YES tier. A list carrying $grants is
#    accepted, so `pf_grant_dictionary(run)` works too.
dict <- pf_grant_dictionary(run$grants, keep = "YES")

#    `exclude` is for the case where the rows you are about to match are rows
#    the dictionary was built from -- a benchmark re-run, say. Without it the
#    dictionary answers those queries with themselves.
#      pf_grant_dictionary(run$grants, exclude = benchmark_ids,
#                          key_col = "grant_id")

# 2. retry only what did not clear, and adopt only what the BMF corroborates
out  <- pf_recover_from_dictionary(run$status, dict, run$recipients,
                                   accept = "agree")

attr(out, "counts")   # retried / dict_yes / agreeing / accepted
attr(out, "queue")    # the uncorroborated claims, for adjudication
```

Three details of placement are deliberate.

**It is a supplement, not a reference.** A dictionary from one run holds the
EINs that run resolved -- 31,721 against the BMF's roughly 1.9M organisations --
and reproduces only 794 of the augmented BMF's 2,979 YES rows, 26.7%. Run as a
reference it is strictly worse, and 37 BMF-YES rows clear to a *different* EIN
against it. It belongs after the cascade or nowhere.

**`keep = "YES"` is the default for a reason.** A dictionary seeded from MAYBE
would propagate exactly the decisions that are in doubt.

**Statistics are not borrowed silently.** The IDF of roughly 90k filer
renderings is not the IDF of 3.88M BMF names, and which one is right is an open
question. `stats = "dictionary"` computes name frequency and token IDF over the
dictionary itself; passing a reference bundle borrows its tables instead. The
argument exists so the two effects are never confounded.

It is **not yet wired into `pf_run()`**. The step on record is to add it as an
optional stage after the cascade, off by default, with the queue surfaced beside
the MAYBE sheet rather than merged into it; until then it is an explicit call,
as above.

# 5. What it is worth

On the cases the BMF left unresolved, as exact-key recall. The unit here is the
benchmark's in-scope **grant row** (4,748 of them: 2,979 YES, 1,044 MAYBE,
725 NO):

```{r}
tab(recall, col.names = c("BMF tier", "dictionary clears", "agreeing with the BMF's top candidate"))
```

End to end through the package API, on the same population at the
**recipient-identity** unit (4,683 identities, of which the BMF run cleared
2,865), after a full augmented-BMF run. The two tables are two units, not two
answers -- that is why the counts differ:

```{r}
tab(endtoend, col.names = c("", "accepted", "clear rate", "queued", "precision"))
```

1,818 unresolved identities were retried and 106 cleared. 42 of those agreed
with the EIN the BMF reference had already surfaced as its own top candidate --
recoverable all along, with the margin gate refusing to release them.

The honest framing of +0.90 points: it is below the "every remaining lever moves
less than 1% of grants" bar the project set for itself, and the trustworthy half
only just reaches it. What makes it worth running anyway is the absolute count
at scale. Roughly 37% of 17.25M grant rows go unresolved, so one point of clear
rate is on the order of **170,000 grants** -- a large number from a rate that
does not move.

# 6. The acceptance rule, and why there is one

**Every EIN in the dictionary came from this pipeline.** Resolving against it
propagates the pipeline's own decisions, errors included, so it is a recall
device whose precision is *inherited* rather than established. That is what
`accept` is for.

* `"agree"` (default) promotes a row only where the dictionary's EIN is the one
  the BMF run already held as its own top candidate. `NA` counts as a
  disagreement, not an agreement: a row the BMF could not name a candidate for
  has nothing to corroborate the dictionary.
* `"all"` promotes every dictionary YES. For measurement, not production -- its
  precision is the unknown that separates +0.90 from +2.26.
* `"none"` annotates and promotes nothing.

The disagreements are not a new failure mode. They concentrate in the known
affiliate problem -- an organisation against its own foundation or alumni fund
(`YALE UNIVERSITY` to `YALE UNIVERSITY ALUMNI FUND`), a chapter network picking
the wrong chapter (`ANY BABY CAN` to a different chapter). That is the same
population the dyad and affiliation work addresses, so the queue lands in work
already underway rather than opening a new front.

Adjudicating one queue is the open step that matters: 64 uncorroborated claims
per 4,748 rows are the only way to turn an inherited precision into a measured
one. The route is the same adjudication the MAYBE tier uses, described in
`vignette("adjudicating-maybe")`.

# 7. It does not get better with scale -- in rate terms

The expectation was large gains once millions of cases have cleared: a 3M-row
dictionary being a substantive database. That was tested directly, with one
fixed query set -- the benchmark's 1,769 unresolved rows -- against nested random
dictionaries from 2% to 100% of the 369,160-row cleared pool.

```{r}
tab(curve, col.names = c("share", "cleared rows", "renderings", "EINs",
                         "rend/EIN", "dict YES", "agreeing", "points",
                         "agreeing per 100k new rows"))
```

**A fifty-fold increase in dictionary rows roughly doubles the recoveries**, 23
to 50, and the last doubling of the dictionary bought two. Raw `dict YES`
saturated outright: 126 at half the pool and 126 at all of it.

The mechanism explains it. Recovery needs a cleared rendering *of the same
organisation*, so the quantity that matters is renderings per organisation --
and that grows logarithmically, 1.265 to 2.798 across a fifty-fold increase in
rows. The tenth foundation to write `USO` adds nothing.

Two corollaries, and the first is easy to get backwards. The **rate** saturates
at about 1.05 points and is reached by half of a single run, so more cleared data
will not raise the percentage. But at full scale the *query* side grows too --
about 6.4M unresolved candidates rather than 1,769 -- so the absolute yield is
large. Build it for the volume, not for the percentage. And because the rate
saturates so early, the pass can be developed and tuned against a small
dictionary without waiting for a full run.

# 8. What none of this establishes

**The precision of `accept = "all"`.** Unknown, and it is exactly the difference
between +0.90 and +2.26 points. The 64 queued cases per 4,748 rows are the
measurement that would settle it.

**That the dictionary's own YES rows are right.** They are the pipeline's
output. Nothing in this pass validates them; it propagates them.

**Which seed a production dictionary should use.** Three candidates, and the
choice is not obvious: the triangulation run's cleared rows (what was measured
here, but drawn from multi-rendering addresses, so it over-represents shared
addresses and probably chapters -- likely *why* the disagreements skew to
affiliates); a corpus-representative run's cleared rows; or the hand-adjudicated
ground truth only, which is tiny but carries no inherited error. The quantity to
choose on is the disagreement rate by seed.

**That the 3.77% coverage figure in section 2 is accuracy.** It is not; 88% of
it survives contest.
